title: First Steps Into Taliban Afghanistan
byline: Originally published as an interview on NomadMania, 21 August 2022
intro: I was the first known traveller to visit Afghanistan since the Taliban takeover in August 2021. Here's the interview I gave about it, and about why I travel the way I do.

qa.q: François please introduce yourself. Where do you come from, where do you live now, what do you do in life…?
a: My name is François-Xavier Paradis-Garneau and I’m from Canada. I was born in the province of Quebec, the French-speaking part of the country, in 1999. I studied English linguistics at the university from 2018 to 2021, the year of my graduation. I studied in that field because I wanted to go teach English abroad, specifically in China and the Middle East.

Due to Covid restrictions, I couldn’t go to China after graduating as I had initially planned in 2018. I had savings from the pandemic working as a part-time security guard. I decided to use my savings to go on a trip and I left Canada in September for an open-ended trip.

qa.q: How do you find that your origins influence you as a traveller? Did being a Canadian help or otherwise influence your travels?
a: Being a Canadian is a net positive for me since I have access to a lot of countries visa-free/visa on arrival. Getting visas is also a lot easier as a Canadian compared to many other countries. I remember in 2018 I was backpacking in China and had been lucky to get a 10-year multi-entry 60-day visa while I met a lot of Europeans who hadn’t had that visa opportunity. They were struggling to extend their single-entry 30-day visas.

I was planning to go to Central Asia and had dismissed the thought of going to Uzbekistan because I’d heard of how difficult it was to get the Letter of Invitation. But then I met an Australian who told me that there had been a change in the visa policy and the visa process no longer required an LOI for certain nationalities including ours.

I applied to the Uzbek embassy in Tajikistan and all I had to give was 50$. I came a few days later to pick up the visa and I remember a Vietnamese lady being told that she had to provide an LOI. I felt very lucky.

On the negative side, some countries are more difficult for me to enter, most notoriously Iran. I would love to visit the country on my own but for the time being, they won’t take me unless I have a tour. I have already had two Iranian visa applications rejected! Overall Canada has a great reputation abroad and people are always happy to meet a Canadian.

qa.q: How did you start travelling and how did that love for travel develop over time?
a: I used to travel as a child with my family, mostly in the USA. I fell in love with long road trips such as driving from Quebec to Florida with my family and looking out the window at the changing landscape. I think that is where the travel bug got me.

I then started travelling by myself in 2017 when I went on a backpacking trip to Europe for 6 weeks. I was blown away. I met dozens of people who shared with me their travel tips to keep their budget low and travel long-term, such as hitchhiking, couchsurfing etc. Some of them were extreme budget travellers who had been travelling for years, dumpster diving and sleeping outside.

Then I realised that my budget could be as low or as high as I wanted and that money was not an obstacle to my travels if I was willing to rough it out. Moreover, I met people in Europe who shared their experiences of travelling outside the West and it intrigued me. Up until that point, I had thought that travelling outside the West was extremely dangerous, difficult and near impossible unless on a tour group. But young people like me had been to India, Oman, Peru, etc.

That made me realise the whole world could be mine to visit if I wanted to and the next year I travelled alone to East and Central Asia. I have always loved history, politics, anthropology and geography and travelling allows me to live out my passions by seeing places in real life instead of through the pages of a book.

qa.q: Do you have any specific travel goals and if yes, what are they? What inspired you to have them?
a: My main travel goal is to acquire a better understanding of the world. I’m quite a curious person and I want to learn more. Travelling allows me to meet the world’s inhabitants and discover their religions, philosophies, etc.

Curiosity is the fuel that keeps me travelling. I find the human species fascinating and travelling allows me to see the full picture. For instance in Pakistan, their family system is completely different from what I’m used to at home. Coming here allows me to see my own culture from their perspective. I like to see things from different angles to have a well-rounded view of humanity.
I’m also travelling to get some interesting stories that I will hopefully be able to share with my children and grandchildren one day around a campfire. For me, my motto is “stories, not stamps”.

qa.q: What are your biggest travel interests? How do you choose your next place to go?
a: I love places that make me feel culturally disoriented. In essence, the less Westernized I hear a country is, the more I will be drawn to it. The more different and exotic a country is compared to Canada, the better. That is why I loved China. I had a complete culture shock there and I enjoyed it.

My biggest travel interests are the people that I meet on the road. I love countries where locals are happy to meet foreigners and discuss with them. I usually choose the next place I will go to based on how friendly I’ve heard the locals are and how culturally interesting the place seems.

I prioritize places that have not totally fallen prey to globalization yet to see them while they are still interesting. Sooner than later everyone on Earth will watch Netflix, drink Coca-Cola and eat at McDonald’s. That day will be the day I stop travelling. I feel like I’m living at the tail end of the golden era of travel. It’s certainly a race against time.

qa.q: You have been to 131 NomadMania regions and ‘only’ 34 UN countries. It seems like you really go in depth when travelling and exploring. Why is that?
a: While I respect country counters, I myself am not chasing a specific number of countries. I’m more interested in stories than in stamps. Therefore when visiting a place I don’t feel the need to rush to tick off a world bucket list. I can take my time.

I usually like seeing a country as thoroughly as possible to really know the place in depth. It is the age-old quality vs quantity debate. I prefer spending one long stretch of time in one country at the expense of not seeing other countries that I’m less interested in.

As for how travel should feel, a good benchmark for me is if I meet someone from a country that I’ve visited and I can sustain a deep conversation about their country. If they seem impressed with my knowledge of their native land then I feel like I’ve done a good job exploring the country.

qa.q: What were some of the biggest surprises – good or bad – that you encountered on your travels so far?
a: One big surprise is how friendly strangers can be if you simply approach them. In China, I was on a bus from Guilin to Longji rice terraces. There was another man on the bus, otherwise empty. I approached him and greeted him. He did not speak English but we communicated through a phone translator. It turned out we were going to the same place. He ended up paying for my entrance fee at the national park and treating me to dinner.

He then gave me his number and told me to contact him when I would come to Chengdu. When I did, he lent me his apartment and went to sleep at his girlfriend’s home for 4 days, to my bewilderment. He drove me around the city, showing me panda reserves, local restaurants, hot springs, and more. All of this would have never happened had I not first initiated contact with him.

The second biggest surprise is that usually the worse the media portrayal and fear factor of a country is, the nicer its inhabitants are — Sudan, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Somaliland. Five years ago I had a negative view of these countries. In my experience it’s been the opposite: they are desperate to give a good image of their country and will do everything they can to help you.

qa.q: Can you tell us the story of how you ended up in Afghanistan? How did you know it would be safe enough, given there was almost no information even among big and extreme travellers?
a: I was exploring Pakistan in the fall of 2021. I entertained the thought of going to Afghanistan after learning that the 4 consulates in Pakistan were now led by the Taliban. I thought it would give more legitimacy to my visa if I got it from a Taliban-controlled consulate. That reassured me.

I then read some blogs from travellers who had been to Afghanistan during the first Taliban government between 1996-2001. It gave me some inspiration. I got in touch with two Iranian photographers who had gone to Afghanistan under the new regime and had both been detained for many days. I knew it would be a bumpy journey, especially for me as a Westerner from a NATO country. I was fully expecting to be arrested at some point.

At the same time, I got a very positive impression from the consul in Peshawar. He assured me that my visit was approved by him and that I was welcome to see the country. In the end, I told myself that someone had to go there first to see how Western travellers would be treated. There’s only so much preparation you can do — at some point you must take a leap of faith, hope for the best, and go.

I was not so concerned about the Taliban harming me. They were now the government and no longer insurgents, desperate for international recognition, with no incentive to harm foreign tourists. My main concern was IS-K, the local Daesh affiliate.

photos.caption: Sharing food with locals in Kabul

qa.q: Would you recommend Afghanistan to other travellers now that you’ve been? Would you consider it safe for women to go?
a: It is possible to visit the country if you have a lot of time on your hands. Be prepared to be detained, questioned, and have a lot of time wasted every day, especially in remote areas like Farah.
The new authorities are still not accustomed to foreign tourists. It will take some time before the country becomes easy and smooth to travel around.
Safety-wise the situation can change very quickly. If you plan to go anywhere, always inquire with locals about the safety of the road ahead. IS-K is still active, albeit weakened.
As for women travellers, I think it should be safe as long as they comply with local rules. I saw foreign female aid workers during my trip, so it should be possible for women to visit as well.

photos.caption: An old tank in Badghis province, near Qala-e-Naw

qa.q: What makes you go to places like Somalia and Afghanistan, rather than somewhere more convenient?
a: I find these countries more rewarding. To use a financial analogy, I get a better return on my investment by going there. Sure, they’re more challenging — visas, logistics, language. But I always learn more from difficult countries.

Their culture is usually better preserved, making them more unique and interesting. I also prefer to do the hardest countries while I’m young and healthy. I’ll still be willing to visit Denmark when I’m 70, but I probably won’t want to do harder countries at that age.

qa.q: How did your general view of the world change with travelling?
a: I realized that humans everywhere on Earth are a lot nicer than the media would make you think. The news is always negative and most people have a fearful view of foreign lands — so did I, before travelling. When I ask people back home if they’d ever go to Sudan, they tell me it’s a no-go area. They’ve never been there; their view is distorted by soundbites. Most people in the world are extremely friendly, and the ones who want to harm you are a small minority.

I no longer take advice about a place from someone who’s never been there. If I had listened to people’s advice I would not have gone to Afghanistan in December 2021, because every Western traveller I met in Pakistan told me it was impossible.
Every country is possible if you have the right strategy and can adapt — dressing locally, avoiding the worst areas. The world is much safer than people think. No country is 100% dangerous.

qa.q: How well do you know your own country? What are some of the most underrated places in Canada?
a: Unfortunately, I don’t know my own country well enough — I’ve mostly spent time visiting foreign countries. Travellers often take their own country for granted. I think the Yukon and the Northwest Territories may be underrated. I’m planning to visit both at some point.

qa.q: Signature question: if you could invite 4 people from any era to dinner, who would your guests be and why?
a: I would probably invite Jesus, Socrates, Mohammed and the Buddha. That should make for an interesting conversation.

title: Where the Road Won't Go: Solo Overlanding the Congo
byline: Originally published on Chasing the Real World, May 28, 2023
intro: Solo trip overland from Angola to Uganda through the DRC. My goal was to visit the DRC far and wide — particularly the Congo basin's jungle areas, tropical rainforest and tributaries — and see if I could cross it South-West to North-East without ever taking an airplane, to see as much on the ground as possible. This report reads like a very, very long blogpost. Buckle up.

editorNote.text: I was the first foreign traveler in Afghanistan after the Taliban takeover. That trip was relatively easy compared to this one.

links.label: BBC video on the Afghanistan trip

sections.heading: Visa
paragraphs: I got my DRC visa in Bujumbura, Burundi. It's not normally possible to get it there as a non-resident. They initially outright refused to process my application. I insisted and asked to speak to higher ups. Eventually I got invited into someone's office and spoke to the right guy who sympathized with me. Speaking French helps, we got friendly. I told him I didn't want to go back to Canada to get the visa when I was so close to the DRC. He said that I could get a visa if I had a letter of invitation “prise en charge”. I got it for 150$ from a local contact. I then came back to the embassy a few days later with the “prise en charge” document and got my DRC visa in less than an hour: 250$, three months multi entry from the day of entry (200$ for single entry three months). I had a three month window to enter the country.

photos.caption: The route: Angola to Uganda through the DRC

sections.heading: From Angola to Kinshasa
paragraphs: After getting my DRC visa in Burundi in June, I carried on travelling through Africa and got to the town of Maqela do Zombo in northern Angola in late August. From there I got a motorbike taxi that agreed to take me to the remote Congolese border of Kimdupulu for about 7 usd. The road there is a sand/dirt track. I was stamped out of Angola — the stamp had barely any ink on it anymore and the old Portuguese building looked like it hadn't been cleaned in 50 years.

Once on the Congolese side I met the Kimdupulu immigration agent who works for the DGM (Direction Générale de Migration), Jean Claude. His office was a wooden cabin. His colleagues from the secret police (ANR) and regular police wanted to investigate me and make issues for me. They asked me to come in their office and to see my passport but Jean-Claude said “passports are the business of DGM, hands off”. He was extremely friendly and invited me to stay in his house for the night. To my surprise he gave me his own bed to sleep in. He even gave me a meal, a SIM card and a beer and didn't ask me a single dollar. He rarely if ever sees foreigners crossing here so he wanted to celebrate with royal hospitality.

The next day I paid a motorbike to get me to Nsangi (20,000 francs; 2,000 francs = 1 usd) and another one to Kisantu (20k). The Kisantu DGM chief told me I had forgotten to pay money for my entrance stamp and should pay him — a bribe — but I befriended him and managed to escape his clutches. I hitchhiked on possibly the only “good” road of the country with a truck to go to Kinshasa. On the way a truck full of cement bags dropped some merchandise and the road was blocked for three hours; people around helped clear out the mess in exchange for payments from the truck driver. I eventually reached Kinshasa at night where my couchsurfing host was waiting for me.

sections.heading: Kinshasa
paragraphs: I didn't stay long in Kinshasa as I was eager to carry on deeper into the country and worried about time constraints. I visited the memorial of the defunct president Laurent Kabila. It's nominally free to visit but my host had to pay a bribe to the guards to let us take pictures. Kinshasa's driving is the most insane I have ever seen, even by African standards — drivers don't care about pedestrians at all. There's an uneasiness in the air. Interesting fact: people dress super well, suit and tie, yet live in shantytowns. It's called “la culture des sapeurs”.

sections.heading: From Kinshasa to Banduduville
paragraphs: I hitchhiked out of Kinshasa with motorbikes and trucks on a good tarmac road until the town of Mongata. I slept there for the night in a villager's barn with his approval, to avoid getting harassed by DGM. The road north of Mongata is not tarmac anymore — a sandy road large enough for trucks to pass, but they can only go at 10-15 km/h.

The next morning when I told the inhabitants I was going to Banduduville, they warned me there was fighting and killings in the area and that buses had stopped going in the last few days. The information was blurry so I decided to try my luck and walk, stopping the occasional motorbike going my direction. There was one army/police checkpoint that was quite nasty and wanted cash, “20$ for registration”. He harassed me so much that my motorbike driver left me there. I tried to leave the barrier on foot but the guy followed me for a kilometer. I turned back, got one inch from his face and said “look man, I know powerful people in Kinshasa near the president. I'll get you fired from your job if you don't leave me alone.” It worked like magic and he ran away. Eventually I got a motorbike lift to Machambio, who hosted me.

The next morning I realized there was a Red Cross team in town and everybody was on alert. This was a full-blown tribal war between the Teke and the Yaka. North of Machambio the Yaka were ethnically cleansing the area of Teke people — slaughtering villagers, burning houses. It was basically genocidal warfare from what they were saying. I was told I shouldn't continue or I'd get killed. Some refugees on foot coming from the red zone told me it should be fine for me since I wasn't a Teke and the Yaka had no motive to kill me. This was the only road to Banduduville anyway, so I decided to continue walking and see how things would turn out.

Five kilometers north of Machambio I stopped at a village, still no traffic northward despite waiting the whole day. I got stuck and slept at the village, fed half-ripe mangoes from the trees. The villagers were incredibly nice, brought me manioc for dinner, and things seemed normal — until one of the guys eating with me told me he'd been part of a Yaka raiding party the day before which had killed four Tekes, including two grandkids. I politely asked him what the point of killing innocent children was and soon realized it wasn't a fruitful conversation.

The next morning I kept walking, getting food and water in the occasional hamlets. Soon I saw burned houses — previously Teke-inhabited villages, completely abandoned. A truck going north refused to take me, blaming “Belgian colonialism and hand cutting”; I told him I was Canadian and we'd never had colonies, but he didn't seem to care. Another truck came and didn't stop, so I ran alongside it in the sand tracks for ten minutes, keeping pace, until the driver's girlfriend had pity on me and convinced him to let me climb onto the roof, on top of the cargo, tied down with ropes. They told me they'd been afraid to take me because there were Yaka roadblocks ahead.

The first one was before the village of Mibe — the guy didn't even notice me, too focused on shaking down the driver for bullet money. Then came the real deal. Right after Mibe we got stopped by fifteen Yaka rebels with carbines and machetes, red turbans, and what looked like black paint over their faces — the driver later told me it's part of a ritual mixing the paint with victims' blood for supernatural power, “fétichisme”. They made everyone get down to check IDs and hunt for any Teke. These guys were high, unmistakably. One saw me and demanded money; I stayed on the roof. I locked eyes with the only one who seemed sober, and he gestured for me to stay put, the most reassuring look I've ever received — “don't worry, it's not you we're after”. Then several of them climbed up onto the roof with their machetes to hitch a ride to their next roadblock. Straight out of a film. We dropped them a few kilometers down and reached Bethanie, then finally Ngadambo at night, across the Kwilu river from Banduduville — no crossing allowed after dark since a local VIP drowned there the year before.

photos.caption: A burned village in Teke-Yaka conflict territory

sections.heading: Banduduville to Kiri
paragraphs: The next morning I tried to board a boat but was harassed by different branches of police threatening to physically remove me if I didn't report to their office. Two hours and a lot of shouting later, I was across, meeting Father Franek, a Polish missionary in the DRC since 2002, who hosted me for free at the Saint Paul mission. From here on the sandy tracks were too narrow for trucks, only bikes. At a river crossing before Bendela, a DGM official mistook my “ordinary” visa category for a missionary visa. In Bendela the authorities forced me into a hotel for the night — they didn't want to miss a football match — so thirty minutes after they left, I pretended to go get food and fled into the pitch-black savannah instead.

I walked and paid my way through Keshu, Cefa, Isaka, and across the river to Nyoki, where I used the line “passports are the business of the DGM, not yours” to fend off the secret police, playing the rival agencies against each other. From Nyoki I took a “baleinière” — a river boat — to Inongo, a two-day journey with a toilet that was a plank of wood with a hole over the lake, and a night spent shipwrecked on a sandbank in a tropical thunderstorm before passengers pushed the boat free by hand. From Inongo I boarded another baleinière, packed shoulder to shoulder with sleeping bodies on the open deck, and reached Kiri without further incident.

photos.caption: Father Franek, a Polish missionary in Banduduville since 2002
With the head of the DGM in Inongo
Packed onto a baleinière river boat

sections.heading: Into the Jungle: Kiri to Monkonto
paragraphs: Kiri is where the real jungle started. I was invited to eat caterpillar soup at a fellow passenger's house and stayed the night at the catholic mission. From there I walked with a companion 60 km to Pendjua, then set out alone to reach Salonga National Park, which meant 90 km on foot to Boyera because the trail wasn't passable by bike. Long stretches were flooded up to my knees, Indiana Jones style, forcing a choice between soaked sneakers or bare feet exposed to parasites. I chose the latter.

I spent the first night 27 km in, taken in by a local pastor whose house was surrounded by hundreds of villagers who, according to him, had never seen a white person since the Belgians left. They stared at me for hours. My host cooked wild boar caught by pygmy hunters — teeming with live worms, which I asked to have boiled first. Two more days of walking through flooded trail and bamboo forest brought me to Boyera on the Momboyo river, where the local police commander, Alain, hosted me after some understandable suspicion.

From Boyera there was no road left, only the river. I hired a pastor and his son to paddle me to Nkassa in a fishing pirogue, lying flat to balance the unstable canoe, six hours upriver. In Nkassa the police commander was a violent drunk the village hated; the local chief begged me to help get him removed. The next morning, a motorized canoe appeared out of nowhere — a priest heading to his church near Salonga, asked by the Nkassa pastor to give me a lift. Twenty-four hours by boat, sleeping aboard, past remote Belgian-era churches, brought me to Wafanya, where the priests fed me monkey — head and brain included, a sign of respect in their culture. I then rode a bike, oiled from the priest's own reserve, to Monkonto.

photos.caption: Villagers who'd never seen a foreigner before

sections.heading: Monkonto, Salonga National Park: To the Bonobos
paragraphs: In Monkonto the phone network didn't work, but an NGO worker had satellite Wi-Fi, my first contact home in two weeks. I was then summoned and aggressively questioned by police and DGM — accused of being a spy — until I played a voice recording from the Wafanya priest vouching for me in Lingala, which finally got me released.

At the Salonga National Park headquarters I learned there was zero tourist infrastructure; I'd be the first tourist to ever show up there. The chief biomonitor, Dieu-Merci, mentioned there were scientists deep in the jungle near Luikotale studying habituated bonobos — unreachable by phone, and visiting without permission was against protocol. I decided my best shot was to make the detour anyway and ask in person.

Getting there took days: a borrowed motorbike to Boleko, a canoe across flooded swampland with an albino ferryman who'd clearly suffered for it (Congolese slang calls albinos “blancs ratés”, failed whitemen), a 17 km night walk using my phone as a flashlight, and — my biggest mistake of the trip — renting a brakeless, gearless bicycle for a planned 60 km leg. It took two days and gave me nerve damage in my right hand that lasted months. From there, motorbikes borrowed and re-borrowed from generous strangers, one machete-cutting a path through fallen trees, got me to the ICCN ranger post at Mundja, where commander Sendi lent me a headtorch for the final stretch to Ipope and then Lumpole.

In Lumpole I met Mara, the Congolese liaison for the bonobo research project, who told me I was lucky: some of the scientists were about to fly out and I could meet them. That night a group came out of the jungle. Barbara, the lead scientist, agreed to let me visit the camp and see the bonobos for free, as a temporary “volunteer”. We trekked 25 km from Lumpole to Luikotale, crossing the Lokoro river. The camp had no anti-venom for the lethal snakes in the area — everyone signs a waiver before entering. I saw flying squirrels, butterflies, small monkeys, and after a few days trekked out with local workers to find the bonobos themselves: watching them eat, play, and move through the canopy in their natural environment, wild bees and biting vines underfoot the whole way.

photos.caption: The bonobo research team deep in Salonga National Park
A bonobo near the Luikotale research camp

sections.heading: From the Bonobos Back to Wafanya
paragraphs: I started feeling sick and weak in Luikotale and left before things got worse. In Ipope I discovered all my cash — over $300 — had been stolen, likely while I was away from my hut. I had just enough left for river crossings, nothing for bikes or food. Back in Mundja, commander Sendi found me visibly ill; a rapid test confirmed malaria. He put me up for three nights through terrible fevers, chased off a drunk village nurse who wanted to give me injections, and at one low point had me message my parents via satellite Wi-Fi, fearing the worst.

To get out, I struck a deal: Sendi's own motorbike and driver would take me 146 km to Bokogombolo, paid for later once I retrieved my hidden cash from under the priest's bed in Wafanya — arranged, remarkably, over WhatsApp, since it turned out Sendi and the priest already knew each other. Weak and still recovering, I helped lift the bike over fallen trees for two days, bartering fruit from villagers along the way since I had almost nothing left to spend. From Bokogombolo, canoes and a lucky lift with a fisherman — who gave me a 1925 Belgian colonial coin he'd dug up in his garden — got me back to Boleko, and eventually to Wafanya, where I paid off my debts and collapsed, exhausted and sick, having also picked up giardia along the way.

photos.caption: A leopard skin gifted by a local chief

sections.heading: From Wafanya to Boende
paragraphs: Doctor Taylor in Wafanya treated my infected blisters, cutting one open to drain it so I could walk again, and loaded me with antibiotics. Once recovered enough, I rented a bike and driver for the 216 km to Boende — which broke down after 76 km. Two overloaded strangers on another bike agreed to squeeze me in anyway for a fraction of the price I'd already paid the first guy. We fell off a few times in the mud but no one was hurt. Boende, the provincial capital, had barely any phone signal, but at least more food options after weeks in the bush.

sections.heading: From Boende to Ikela
paragraphs: I hailed motorbikes directly on the roadside rather than renting one, cheaper that way, and eventually rode 326 km to Ikela over three nights and four days with two high-ranking Tshuapa civil servants, sleeping at villagers' homes along the way per local custom. We hit several illegal wooden roadblocks where locals demanded payment for “road work” no one could point to; one standoff with fifty aggressive villagers lasted thirty tense minutes before my companions' government IDs got us through without paying.

Arriving in Ikela sick with a 40-degree fever, I was held for 45 minutes by DGM and army officials just looking at my passport. When they wouldn't give it back, I snapped it out of the officer's hands and told him I was done playing games and needed a hospital. He was furious; I opened my arms and told him the worst he could do was shoot me and dump my body in the river, and that everyone present, including my two friends, was a witness. I photographed his ID, told him my “powerful friends in Kinshasa” would hear about this, and walked away. They didn't follow. I got treated at the hospital and rested at a friend's home for a few days.

sections.heading: Ikela to Kisangani
paragraphs: Hitchhiking onward toward Opala, I passed armed FARDC soldiers who let me go after I told them I had nothing for them, and a drunk checkpoint commander who backed off once I played a recorded vouching message in Lingala. My driver that stretch casually told me he'd once raped a woman, and that it was common — a grim window into the realities some people live with there.

From near Opala, a young man transporting a goat to sell in Kisangani took me the rest of the way for a fee, goat included, biting at my hand from its perch on the bike. Checkpoints got worse as we went: a legitimate DGM post, then working villagers I happily tipped for actually repairing the road, then a nasty army-and-agency checkpoint that harassed my driver for hours over an expired license until he handed over his motorbike torchlight as a bribe. Twenty kilometers from Kisangani, tax officials demanded a “foreigner's tax” I refused to pay; we were eventually let through, but by then it was pitch dark and we'd lost our only light, so I rode the last stretch by phone-flashlight at a crawl.

sections.heading: Kisangani
paragraphs: Kisangani has no real supermarket but decent restaurants, and I met Jean Pierre (Giampetro Valenti), an Italian former missionary who's lived in the DRC since 1981 and never left, even through the worst of the wars. He hosted me and had more stories than anyone I've met. The city's infrastructure was a mess while I was there: no reliable electricity, water only at night for a few hours, generator operators charging to charge a phone.

At the Boyoma Falls I was swarmed by thirty teenagers demanding $50 for a five-second look, pressing against me until two off-duty ANR officers intervened, escorted me past the crowd for free, then drove me to their base to be searched and, ultimately, asked for money themselves. I walked away. My advice: the falls aren't worth the hassle alone; go with a local who can speak for you, or skip it.

photos.caption: Jean Pierre Valenti, an Italian missionary in Kisangani since 1981

sections.heading: Kisangani to Epulu, Okapi Reserve
paragraphs: East of Kisangani, trucks finally appear, hauling oil in from Kenya, meaning an actual break from motorbikes. But first, a checkpoint 28 km out turned me back to Kisangani's DGM office, where I was told the road east was too dangerous due to rebel activity and I should fly instead. I heard the warning and went anyway on foot and by bike, sneaking past checkpoints in a hoodie, riding through a stretch known for “coupeurs de route” bandits at night without incident, and eventually linking up with a convoy of Somali truckers headed for Uganda.

The truckers explained the real danger: the ADF, an ISIS-affiliated rebel group active on the road between Mambasa and Komanda, known for burning vehicles and kidnapping drivers for ransom. Some trucking companies still risked the shorter Mambasa route with a paid army escort; others rerouted north through Isiro and Aru. I split off with the group heading toward Epulu, which sat just inside the safer margin.

sections.heading: Epulu, Okapi Reserve: Disaster Strikes
paragraphs: In Epulu I arranged, through the reserve's ICCN and WWF staff, to spend three nights in the forest with a Mbuti pygmy community, hunting with spears and nets, for about $100 all in. The deal was set, the mood was good. Then everything changed. I was summoned to the ANR secret police, interrogated for an hour in a manner unlike any prior checkpoint, formally, with notes taken, and then two men in anti-terrorism gear arrived with machine guns and asked if I'd ever been arrested in Afghanistan.

It clicked immediately. A year earlier I'd been briefly detained by the Taliban in Farah province, and a Canadian news segment had since misreported it as an ISIS suspicion, a claim never actually made by the Taliban or the original local reporting. Maxime, the reserve's French head of security, had served in Afghanistan against the Taliban and, on hearing I'd been there, apparently decided I was linked to the ADF or ISIS. I was searched item by item, treated as if my electric razor and padlock were explosives, and by evening placed under armed guard outside my hotel room, unable to leave, given no explanation.

I got the Canadian embassy on the phone that night, and again in the morning, only to find a local staffer with no real authority and no urgency. I was told I couldn't leave Epulu because the Mambasa territorial administrator wanted to meet me and possibly transfer me toward Mambasa itself, deep in ADF territory, which was the last place I wanted to go. I bluffed my way through it: telling the local police my embassy was “furious” and threatening media attention if I wasn't released (they weren't, and I wasn't planning to), and getting the administrator's direct phone number from the sympathetic Epulu police commander. I fed that number to the embassy staffer and let the threat of a phone call from “the Canadian government” do the rest.

It worked. The administrator backed off the next day, and the police released me with written confirmation of my innocence. But the Okapi Reserve staff never let me rejoin the pygmy trip, Maxime refused to meet me again, and the community's chief, who badly needed the money, was told he'd be arrested if he took me into the forest anyway.

photos.caption: At the police post in Epulu, during the detention

sections.heading: Epulu to Uganda
paragraphs: I hitchhiked back out with the Somali truckers, slept a night in a hotel that turned out to double as a brothel in Nya-Nya, and talked my way past a checkpoint the next morning by calling the Mambasa administrator directly and putting him on speaker. North of Nya-Nya the entire mood of the country shifted: friendlier checkpoints, better roads, a DGM officer who just wanted my phone number instead of a bribe, and jungle giving way to open savanna.

Rides with a diamond trader, then a group of VIP Congolese in a 4x4, brought me toward Watsa and Durba, gold-mining country with a reputation for nighttime violence. A brief stop let me watch a pygmy hunter harvest wild honey by hand, smoking out the bees, before his wife came running, terrified I'd harm him. From Durba it was 176 km to Aru, on the Ugandan border. At the DRC exit post an official tried to arrest me for having gotten my visa in a non-resident country, a threat I talked down using recorded voice messages of local references, the same trick that had worked the whole trip.
Then I crossed into Uganda and was greeted with a smile and “Welcome to Uganda, sir.” I was in another world.

photos.caption: One of many river crossings along the way

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: If you read this whole thing, you now have a good idea of the challenges that await you if you travel through the DRC overland. It's a beautiful country with amazing nature and wildlife. The local people are, overall, friendly and hospitable. It was a tough journey — logistics, health, fear — but it also showed me the best of people through everyone who helped and hosted me along the way. Don't do this overland alone if you're a pushover. If you're easily intimidated, don't do it. There will be moments you're afraid; don't show it. Stay tough no matter what. You will not be the same after crossing the DRC overland.
